title: The painted timber houses of Odunpazarı
tagline: A hill of ochre, blue and rose Ottoman houses with their upper floors leaning over the lanes — the town Eskişehir grew out of, and still the first walk.
when: a weekday morning, or late afternoon as the lamps come on
why: Odunpazarı — the name means 'wood market' — is the slope on the southern edge of the plain where Eskişehir began, and the old quarter there holds one of the best-kept runs of Ottoman timber houses in central Anatolia: two-storey, brightly painted, with the upper floor jutting out over the street on carved brackets. The district restored the core street by street from the 2000s — around 300 houses, three mosques, two caravanserais and fifteen fountains across some thirty lanes — and in 2012 Turkey put the 'Odunpazarı Historical Urban Site' on its UNESCO World Heritage tentative list. Today the houses are homes, cafés, small museums, glass and meerschaum workshops and boutique hotels, and the quarter holds the Contemporary Glass Arts Museum, opened in 2007 in three restored houses with Anadolu University as Turkey's first museum of its kind.
take: This is the walk we do with every newcomer, and it works best with no plan: climb in from Atatürk Bulvarı, let the colours pull you up the lanes, and stop wherever someone is working in a doorway. Mornings are the quiet time; on weekends the main lanes fill with day-trippers off the Istanbul and Ankara trains, so go early or go late. Sit down for tea in a konak courtyard rather than buying another magnet. Be honest with visitors about what it is: a careful restoration, polished in places, but lived in all the same. The museums and the mosque complex below have their own entries — save at least one for a second visit.

title: Kurşunlu, the meerschaum museum and the carvers of Atlıhan
tagline: A sixteenth-century mosque complex under lead domes, and the soft white stone the city carves into pipes.
when: a weekday, outside prayer times for the mosque
why: At the foot of Odunpazarı stands the Kurşunlu complex, built between 1517 and 1525 for Çoban Mustafa Paşa, a vizier of Selim I and Süleyman the Magnificent; the 'leaded' name comes from the lead-covered domes. The architect is not known for certain — it is attributed to Acem Ali, the chief architect before Sinan, not to Sinan himself. Around the mosque are the old medrese, kitchens, guest rooms and a Mevlevi lodge that housed the whirling dervishes for centuries, and inside the complex the Odunpazarı municipality runs a museum of lületaşı — meerschaum, the soft white sepiolite mined by hand from deep shafts on the plain around the city and carved into pipes, beads and figures. Eskişehir's mines are the world's best-known source of it, and Eskişehir meerschaum is a registered geographical indication. Next door, the restored Atlıhan caravanserai is a bazaar of crafts and meerschaum workshops.
take: Do the mosque courtyard first, then the meerschaum museum — it's small, and the master carvers' pipes (sultans, lions, bearded heads, whole scenes in one stone) are startling up close. Then cross to Atlıhan and find a workshop where someone is actually carving; most will talk you through it and show you how raw meerschaum looks like a lump of chalk. If you want to buy, a real carved pipe is not a cheap souvenir — be wary of very low prices, and ask how the stone was finished. The craft is ageing; the carvers will tell you they struggle to find apprentices, which is a good reason to buy from them directly. Cover shoulders and knees in the mosque.

title: Odunpazarı Modern Museum (OMM)
tagline: Kengo Kuma's stack of timber boxes in the middle of the Ottoman quarter — a serious contemporary art museum in a city of students.
when: a weekday afternoon; closed on Mondays
why: OMM opened in September 2019 to house the contemporary art collection of the collector Erol Tabanca. The building is by the Japanese firm Kengo Kuma and Associates: timber volumes stacked and shifted on top of each other, drawing on the old houses around it, on Ottoman domes and on Japanese joinery — and on the timber market that gave Odunpazarı its name. Inside are three floors of galleries around a tall central atrium, a café and a shop, with exhibitions of Turkish and international artists drawn from the collection and from loans. The current exhibition, 'Echoes of the Earth', runs from 26 September 2026 to 12 September 2027.
take: Go for the building as much as the art — stand in the atrium and look up, then walk round the outside and see how the boxes sit among the old roofs. It is the best indoor plan in the city for a cold or rainy afternoon, and the café is a good place to meet a new friend who doesn't want a bar. Pair it with the old town and you have the classic Eskişehir first day. It's closed on Mondays, and ticket prices and hours are on omm.art — check before you go; children under twelve get in free. Groups of twenty or more are asked to contact the museum in advance, which matters if you're organising a Smileys outing.

title: Çibörek, the city's Crimean Tatar pastry
tagline: A thin half-moon pastry with raw mince sealed inside, fried in seconds so the meat steams in its own juice — eat it with your hands and lean forward.
when: lunch, or the first stop of an evening
why: Eskişehir has one of Turkey's largest Crimean Tatar communities, descended from the waves of migration out of Crimea after the Crimean War in the 1850s and 60s, and çibörek (çiğ börek, literally 'raw börek') is the dish they brought with them. A disc of very thin dough is filled with raw minced meat, onion, salt and black pepper, folded into a crescent and fried in hot oil for under a minute a side, so the filling cooks in its own steam and the juice stays inside. Eskişehir çiğ böreği was registered as a geographical indication in 2012 on the Chamber of Commerce's application, and the registration describes the traditional serving: hot, five to a portion, eaten by hand.
take: Order a portion and an ayran and eat it straight away — çibörek gets sad in ten minutes. Hold it by the edge and take the first bite carefully: the juice is hot and it will go down your wrist if you're not ready. The best places are the plain, busy ones with a Tatar name over the door; ask a member for this year's favourite rather than trusting a list. Some places also do a cheese or potato version for vegetarians, but the meat one is the point. It's cheap enough to be our default 'meet before the main plan' food.

title: The Porsuk: footbridges, boats and the riverside evening
tagline: A slow river through the middle of town, crossed by a dozen footbridges, with tour boats, gondolas and half the city walking beside it after dark.
when: early evening, from the golden hour into the first lights
why: The Porsuk river runs straight through the city centre, dividing the Odunpazarı side from Tepebaşı, and since the early 2000s the metropolitan municipality has turned its banks into the city's living room: landscaped banks, footbridges every few hundred metres, cafés along the water, and the Adalar — the river-island stretch lined with bars and terraces. Since 2009 the municipality has run boat tours and Venetian-style gondolas from the Köprübaşı pier, which carried more than 300,000 people between January 2024 and May 2025. The first International Porsuk Festival took over the riverbanks and Kentpark with free concerts and events on 2–6 September 2026.
take: The river is the reason Eskişehir feels so easy to live in: you walk everywhere along it, and everyone else does too. Do the boat once — it's short, cheap and a nice way to see the bridges from below — and the gondola only if you're in a couple or a group of four and want the photo. The better plan is free: walk the banks from Köprübaşı towards the Adalar as the light goes, stop for tea on whichever terrace has space, and drift on to dinner. Boat times change with the season and the weather, so check at the pier. If the festival returns next September, it's the best free weekend in the city — watch the municipality's announcements for dates.

title: Barlar Sokağı and the Adalar: the student night out
tagline: A bar street in a city of students — cheap pints, live bands, shouting over music and a crowd that is mostly under thirty.
when: a term-time Thursday to Saturday from 9pm; quieter in summer
why: Eskişehir is one of Turkey's best-known student cities: Anadolu, Eskişehir Osmangazi and Eskişehir Technical universities together have tens of thousands of students in a city of under a million, and they shape its nights. The centre of it is Vural Sokak in Hoşnudiye, just north of the river, which everyone calls Barlar Sokağı — 'Bars Street' — a short street and its side lanes packed with pubs, rock bars and small live-music venues, busiest from Thursday to Saturday in term. A few minutes away, the bars and terraces along the Adalar on the Porsuk are the slightly older, slightly calmer version of the same night.
take: Start on the river at the Adalar for a first drink outside, then walk up to Barlar Sokağı once it fills, around ten. Go with two or three people and pick a bar with live music; this is where Eskişehir's international students and the local ones mix most easily, and it's a cheap night out by any standard. Be clear-eyed about the downsides: it is loud, crowded and young, the late hours can get rowdy, and the street is a recurring political argument in the city, so the scene shifts from year to year. Leave before the last-hour crowd, keep your phone in a front pocket; if you'd rather talk than shout, the river bars are the better half of the night. Summer, when the students go home, is much quieter.

title: Balaban, met helvası and the rest of the Eskişehir table
tagline: Meatballs on butter-soaked bread under tomato and yogurt, a pulled halva that isn't the tahini kind, and a simit with its own protected name.
when: lunch for balaban; helva with afternoon tea
why: Beyond çibörek, the city has a short, distinctive table. Balaban kebabı is its plate for a hungry lunch: small grilled köfte laid on cubes of pide, covered with tomato sauce and yogurt, with melted butter poured over the top — related to İskender in shape, but with köfte in place of döner. Met helvası is the sweet, and it is not the sesame halva most people know: flour is roasted slowly in oil, then pulled together with boiled sugar syrup by a team of hands until it turns into fine strands, and cut into short, fibrous sticks. It was registered as a geographical indication in 2017, and its name comes from 'met', an old children's game played with sticks — the loser, the story goes, had to make the helva. The Eskişehir simidi, crisp and heavy with sesame, joined the protected list in 2022.
take: Do balaban at lunch in a plain esnaf lokantası or a kebab house that lists it by name — order it for yourself, it's not a sharing dish, and come hungry. Buy met helvası by the box from a helva shop in the centre and eat it with tea; it's lighter than it looks and very sweet, so don't plan on more than a couple of sticks. A simit in the morning from a street cart is the cheapest good thing in the city. We name no restaurants on purpose — Eskişehir's food scene turns over fast with the student calendar, so ask in the group what's good this term.

title: Hamamyolu and the hot-water baths
tagline: A long pedestrian park strip over the city's hot springs, with old neighbourhood hamams on either side — the centre's everyday evening walk.
when: an evening walk any time; a hamam on a cold afternoon
why: Eskişehir sits on shallow hot water, which comes up only a few tens of metres below the street in the old Sıcaksular — 'hot waters' — area, and people have bathed in it since Roman and Byzantine times. Hamamyolu Caddesi, once called Yunak Caddesi, runs through the middle of it: today a long, traffic-free park strip with water channels, cafés and benches. Along it and in the streets around are the city's traditional bathhouses, a handful of which still draw on the thermal water, alongside the cobblers and shoe-shiners the street has always had.
take: Treat Hamamyolu as the walk you do without thinking about it — it's how locals cross the centre, and on a summer evening it is full of families and couples. The hamam is the interesting part: on a winter afternoon, a hot-water bath in an old neighbourhood hamam is a very Eskişehir thing to do and costs far less than a hotel spa. Men's and women's sections, hours and prices vary from bath to bath, and not every hamam on the street uses thermal water, so ask at the door before you pay. Bring flip-flops and your own towel to be safe.

title: Sazova Park and the fairy-tale castle
tagline: A castle of 26 towers, a pirate ship on a lake, a Japanese garden and a zoo — the city's weekend park, unashamedly playful.
when: a weekday afternoon, or a spring or autumn weekend
why: Sazova Science, Culture and Art Park opened in 2008 on some 400 decares on the western side of Tepebaşı, and it is the municipality's most ambitious park: an artificial lake with a full-size pirate ship moored in it, a Japanese garden, a zoo, a miniature railway, a science experiment centre and a planetarium, a miniature park of Turkic monuments, and cafés and lawns around them. Its centrepiece is the Masal Şatosu, the fairy-tale castle, opened in March 2014 — 26 towers modelled on towers and minarets from around Turkey. In the Ramadan holiday of 2026 alone the castle had more than 12,000 visitors.
take: Adults roll their eyes at the castle and then take forty photos of it — go with that. The park itself is free to walk in and genuinely pleasant: do a loop of the lake, sit in the Japanese garden, and save the paid attractions for when you have kids or visitors in tow. Weekends and holidays are packed with families; a weekday afternoon is calm. It's a short ride west of the centre — check the Estram app for the nearest stop. Good for a relaxed Smileys picnic in spring, when the lawns are green and the steppe wind has dropped.

title: A night with the city symphony or the City Theatres
tagline: A municipal orchestra and a theatre company that fill their halls all season — Eskişehir's culture-city reputation, earned on stage.
when: the season runs from early autumn to late spring
why: Eskişehir calls itself a culture city, and its metropolitan municipality backs that with its own symphony orchestra and its own theatre company. In 2025 the Eskişehir Metropolitan Municipality Symphony Orchestra gave 38 symphonic concerts to more than 43,000 listeners, plus jazz and chamber nights, and the City Theatres staged 25 productions over 257 performances for more than 72,000 people, and ran their international children's, youth and puppet theatre festival in May. Both are paid for by the city rather than the state, which is a large part of why a town of students has the cultural calendar of a much bigger place.
take: Make it a monthly group ritual: a concert, then a drink by the river. The symphony is the easy one for newcomers — no language needed — and the opera-and-operetta nights are the friendliest way into classical music we know. The City Theatres play in Turkish, so pick a comedy or a musical if your Turkish is new, and go with a member who can explain the jokes at the interval. Popular nights can sell out, and programmes, prices, venues and ticketing are on the municipality's website — check which hall your ticket is for before you set off.

title: The Yılmaz Büyükerşen Wax Museum
tagline: Two hundred wax figures, most of them sculpted by the city's own long-serving mayor — gloriously odd and very Eskişehir.
why: Yılmaz Büyükerşen was Eskişehir's metropolitan mayor for twenty-five years, from 1999 to 2024, and he is also a sculptor — he made wax figures of Atatürk long before he made a museum of them. The wax museum he founded opened on Atatürk Bulvarı in Odunpazarı on 19 May 2013, billed as Turkey's first, and is run by the metropolitan municipality: around two hundred figures in five themed halls, from Atatürk and the War of Independence to Turkish politicians, writers, actors, singers and Eskişehir's sports heroes, and Hollywood stars, most of them modelled by Büyükerşen himself. Ticket income goes to education for girls and for children with disabilities. It was busy as ever over the 2026 Ramadan holiday.
take: Go in the right mood — this is not Madame Tussauds, it's one man's very personal gallery of the people who mattered to him and to the republic, and that's what makes it charming. Spend most of your time in the Atatürk and Turkish halls; the domestic figures are the ones that make Turkish friends laugh and argue, which is the real fun of going with a group. An hour is plenty. It closes on Mondays, and hours and prices are worth checking before you go. Combine it with OMM and the old town on the same walk.

title: The Devrim car, Turkey's first homemade automobile
tagline: The car railway engineers built in about four and a half months in 1961 — and the story of the hundred metres that made it famous.
when: a weekday or weekend; closed on Mondays
why: In 1961 President Cemal Gürsel ordered a fully domestic car, and engineers at the state railway factory in Eskişehir — today TÜRASAŞ — designed and built four of them, from engine to body, in about four and a half months, in time for Republic Day on 29 October. The cars went to Ankara by train with their tanks emptied for safety, and when Gürsel climbed in, the black Devrim ran dry after about a hundred metres; the newspapers never let it go, and the project was shelved. One Devrim survives, and since March 2018 it has been the centrepiece of a museum inside the TÜRASAŞ works, with the tools, drawings and parts used to make it and a group of old steam locomotives.
take: Even if you don't care about cars, go for the story — it's a parable every Turk knows, about ambition, bureaucracy and bad luck, and standing next to the actual car makes it land. Ask a Turkish friend to tell you their version; everyone has one. The museum sits inside a working industrial site, so allow time to find the entrance, and check opening days and the ticket price before you go — it's closed on Mondays. A good rainy-day pair with the wax museum.

title: A sand beach in the middle of Anatolia
tagline: Three hundred and fifty metres of real sea sand, a lake, an Olympic pool and sunloungers — hours from the nearest coast.
when: a weekday in July or August, from opening time
why: Kentpark is a 300,000-square-metre park the metropolitan municipality built along the Porsuk east of the centre, and its most famous feature is an artificial beach: about 350 metres of sea sand trucked in from the coast, laid along a lake, with two open-air Olympic-size pools beside it, one for children. Sunloungers, umbrellas, showers and lockers come with the entry ticket, and lifeguards are on duty. The beach runs in the summer only — in 2025 the season opened on 4 July, with the facilities open seven days a week through the daytime. The rest of Kentpark — lawns, paths and play areas around the water — is a free city park all year, with its own tram stop.
take: It sounds like a gimmick and it is one, a bit — but on a 35-degree August day on the plateau, a lounger on warm sand and a swim is exactly right, and it's one of the most relaxed group days we do. Go on a weekday and arrive at opening; weekends are crowded and loud with families. The season is short and the dates move from year to year, so check the municipality's announcements before you plan around it. Outside summer, the park is still a lovely flat walk or run beside the river.

title: Seyitgazi and Midas City: a Phrygian Valley day
tagline: A hilltop Seljuk shrine to a legendary warrior, then a seventeen-metre temple façade the Phrygians carved into a cliff for their mother goddess.
when: a dry spring or autumn day; avoid deep winter on the plateau roads
why: Drive south out of the city and the steppe turns into the volcanic tuff country the Phrygians settled nearly three thousand years ago. About forty-five kilometres out, Seyitgazi's hillside complex was founded in 1207–08 by Ümmühan Hatun, mother of the Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Keykubad I, around the tomb of Seyyid Battal Gazi — an eighth-century Arab warrior killed fighting Byzantium who became the hero of Turkish epic tales; it later became a Bektashi lodge and was enlarged under Bayezid II. Further south, in Yazılıkaya village in the Han district, is Midas City and its Midas Monument: a seventeen-metre façade cut into the rock, with a niche for a statue of the mother goddess Cybele and a Phrygian inscription naming Midas. It is a temple front, not a tomb; scholars date it anywhere from the eighth to the sixth century BC. Turkey added 'Mountainous Phrygia' to its UNESCO tentative list in 2015, and Anadolu University resumed excavations at the site in 2022.
take: This needs a car — share one between four and make a day of it: Seyitgazi in the morning, a village lunch, then the afternoon at Midas City, where the low sun brings out the carved patterns on the façade. Walk up past the monument onto the plateau behind it for the rock-cut remains and the view; the waymarked Phrygian Way hiking routes all end here, if you get hooked. Dress modestly at Seyitgazi — it is a working shrine and pilgrims visit. There is little shade and few facilities at Midas City, so bring water and food, and check road conditions in winter. Ask in the group: someone usually has a car and a free Saturday.

title: Sivrihisar's forest of wooden columns
tagline: Sixty-seven wooden columns holding up a Seljuk mosque on the Ankara road — Eskişehir's first UNESCO World Heritage listing.
when: a weekday, outside prayer times; Fridays are busy
why: Sivrihisar is a small hill town about a hundred kilometres east of Eskişehir on the road to Ankara, under a jagged ridge of rock. Its Ulu Cami was built in 1232 under the Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Keykubad I and rebuilt in 1274, and inside it is one of the largest wooden hypostyle halls in Anatolia: 67 timber columns of juniper and pine holding a flat timber roof, several of them topped with stone capitals reused from older buildings — local tradition says from Pessinus, the ancient sanctuary of Cybele about sixteen kilometres away. In 2023 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with four other wooden-columned medieval mosques of Anatolia, the first World Heritage site in Eskişehir province. Tradition also makes Sivrihisar's district the birthplace of Nasreddin Hoca, the folk joker of a thousand stories.
take: Go mid-morning, step inside, and let your eyes adjust — the light falls through the high windows onto the columns and it feels more like a wood than a building. Find the carved walnut minbar and look closely at the column capitals. It is a working mosque, so visit outside prayer times, cover up and take your shoes off. Then walk the old lanes of the town and up towards the rocks for the view. With a car you can add Pessinus at Ballıhisar on the same day; by public transport, take an Ankara-bound bus and ask to be let off at Sivrihisar.
